title: The rāsa-līlā in the Harivaṃśa, Viṣṇu Purāṇa and Bhāgavata
subject: narr:rasa-lila
question: How does each text tell Kṛṣṇa's nocturnal dance with the gopīs?

rows.statement: Short erotic description: on autumn nights Kṛṣṇa delights the young cowherd women, who sing his deeds in rows and pairs, imitate him and cling to him; no flute, no disappearance, no search, and the constituted text does not use the word rāsa (63.25, 63.35 'adorned with circles of gopīs').

sources.edition: Vaidya CE (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: Kṛṣṇa's song draws the gopīs; he vanishes; they act out his deeds and follow his footprints and those of a favoured gopī; he reappears and forms the rāsa-maṇḍala, holding each gopī by the hand; the chapter closes by declaring him the all-pervading Self.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Five chapters: the flute call, Kṛṣṇa's test of the gopīs, his disappearance at their pride, the search and footprints of one favoured gopī, the Gopī-gīta, the reunion, and the rāsa with Kṛṣṇa multiplied between each pair of women (10.33.3); Parīkṣit asks how the upholder of dharma could do this (10.33.26–37).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

rows.statement: Reproduces the Viṣṇu Purāṇa account almost verbatim (rāsa-goṣṭhī, rāsa-maṇḍala).

sources.edition: Brahmapurāṇa 1–246, Tübingen Purāṇa Project (P. Schreiner, R. Söhnen-Thieme); GRETIL e-text

note: The sequence HV → ViP → BhP is generally read as successive elaboration (Hardy 1983; Schweig 2005); the Brahma Purāṇa copies the ViP. The named favourite, Rādhā, is absent from all four.

title: Where the Syamantaka jewel came from and how long Kṛṣṇa fought Jāmbavān
subject: narr:syamantaka
question: Who first obtained the jewel, from where, and how long did the fight with Jāmbavān last?

rows.statement: Prasena obtained the jewel 'from the ocean' as Dvāravatī was being founded; the story of the Sun giving it to Satrājit is a star (inserted) passage after 28.12. Kṛṣṇa fought Jāmbavān in the cave 'with his arms alone' for twenty-one days.

sources.edition: Vaidya CE (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: The Sun (Vivasvat) takes the jewel from his own neck and gives it to his friend Satrājit; the fight lasts twenty-one days.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Prasena(jit) obtained it 'from the Sun' (sūryād), with the Sun episode in the constituted text.

sources.edition: Brahmapurāṇa 1–246, Tübingen Purāṇa Project (P. Schreiner, R. Söhnen-Thieme); GRETIL e-text
sources.quote: divyaṃ syamantakaṃ nāma sa sūryād upalabdhavān

rows.statement: The Sun, pleased with Satrājit, gives him the jewel; Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavān fight for twenty-eight days (aṣṭā-viṃśa-aham), and Jāmbavān recognises his lord Rāma; in 10.83.10 Jāmbavatī says twenty-seven days.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

note: The critical Harivaṃśa's 'from the ocean' reading versus the Sun-gift in the Viṣṇu, Brahma and Bhāgavata Purāṇas suggests the solar origin entered with later redaction; the HV vulgate includes it.

title: Order and form of Kṛṣṇa's infant exploits
subject: char:krishna
question: Which infancy episodes does each text tell, and in what form?

rows.statement: Cart overturned (50.4–19), then Pūtanā as a night-bird (50.20–24); then the binding to the mortar and the twin trees (51). No Tṛṇāvarta, Agha or Brahmā episode.

sources.edition: Vaidya CE (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: Pūtanā (5.5), then the cart (5.6.1–8), the binding and the trees (5.6.9–20). No Tṛṇāvarta.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Pūtanā (10.6), the cart and Tṛṇāvarta (10.7), butter-stealing and the universe in Kṛṣṇa's mouth (10.8), the binding (10.9) and the cursed yakṣas (10.10), then Vatsa, Baka (10.11), Agha (10.12) and Brahmā's theft (10.13–14).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

rows.statement: Lists Pūtanā, the twin arjunas and the cart, then Kāliya, in a brief digest.

sources.edition: Rajendralal Mitra ed. (Bibliotheca Indica 1870–79); GRETIL e-text

title: The burning of Tripura in the Mahābhārata, Matsya, Liṅga, Śiva and Bhāgavata
subject: narr:tripura-dahana
question: Who builds and defends the three cities, and what part does Viṣṇu play in their destruction?

rows.statement: The three sons of Tāraka receive from Brahmā cities of gold, silver and iron, built by Maya; Hari, son of Tārakākṣa, makes a pool that revives the dead. The gods build a chariot of the cosmos with Brahmā as charioteer; Viṣṇu, Soma and Agni form the arrow, and Śiva burns the cities with one shot. Told by Duryodhana as a model for Śalya's charioteership.

sources.edition: BORI Critical Edition (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: Maya is the protagonist, builder and war-leader; Keśava in bull form drinks the nectar pond (136.63–65) and Śiva's arrow burns the cities; Maya's house survives in the ocean (140.75–78).

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: The asuras are pious Śiva-worshippers; Viṣṇu by his māyā creates an obstacle to their dharma (1.71.71–74) so that Śiva may destroy them.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Viṣṇu creates a shaven-headed teacher who converts the Tripura asuras to a 'Jina'/Arhat doctrine (2.5.4–5); Śiva first worships Gaṇeśa (2.5.10.7–14), then burns the cities; Maya, a devotee, is spared and given Vitala (2.5.12).

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

rows.statement: Told within the Prahlāda book: Maya's reviving well; Viṣṇu as a cow, with Brahmā as the calf, drinks it dry; Śiva burns the cities.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

note: The motif of Viṣṇu destroying the demons' religion appears in several Purāṇas in Buddhist or Jain dress (cf. the 'māyāmoha' of ViP 3.17–18); it reflects sectarian polemic, not a historical event.

title: Who kills Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and how?
subject: narr:madhu-kaitabha
question: Which deity kills the two demons born during Viṣṇu's cosmic sleep, and what is the decisive device?

rows.statement: Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa) alone; the demons grant him a boon and ask to die where there is no covering; he beheads them with the discus on his bare thighs.

sources.edition: BORI Critical Edition (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: The demons steal the Vedas from Brahmā; Viṣṇu as Hayaśiras (horse-head) recovers them; the demons then fight Nārāyaṇa, who kills them.

sources.edition: BORI Critical Edition (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: Viṣṇu kills them on the single ocean; their fat (medas) forms the earth, hence 'Medinī'.

sources.edition: Vaidya CE (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: Brahmā praises the Goddess as Yoganidrā; she leaves Viṣṇu's eyes, he wakes and kills the demons — the Goddess is the enabling power and the first carita's true subject.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

rows.statement: Prahlāda's hymn: in the form of Hayaśiras Viṣṇu killed the Veda-stealing Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

title: How the androgynous Śiva (Ardhanārīśvara) originates
subject: narr:ardhanarishvara-origin
question: Why and how does Śiva appear as half-man, half-woman?

rows.statement: Rudra springs from Brahmā's angry brow with a body half woman, half man; told to divide himself, he separates the female and male and multiplies each.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Same account of Rudra born half-woman from Brahmā.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

rows.statement: Same pattern: Rudra appears as ardhanārīnaravapu at creation.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Mahādeva, born as Brahmā's son, becomes Ardhanārīśvara, bright as the rising sun, and the female half is given to creation.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Brahmā cannot make creation increase because no women exist; he worships Śiva, who appears as Ardhanārīśvara and separates the Goddess from his body; Brahmā asks her to be born as Dakṣa's daughter.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay), books 1 and 7; GRETIL e-text

note: The androgyne appears in sculpture from the Kuṣāṇa period at Mathurā; the textual aetiologies are later and differ on whether the androgyne is a birth-form of Rudra or a theophany of the supreme Śiva.

title: Who takes the poison of the churning?
subject: narr:nilakantha
question: What happens to the poison that rises from the churned ocean?

rows.statement: Constituted text: no poison episode. Passages in the critical apparatus (App. I after 1.16.15 and 1.16.27; *268, *274) have Rudra drink the hālāhala and become Nīlakaṇṭha.

sources.edition: BORI Critical Edition (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: No poison episode in the constituted text.

sources.edition: Baroda Critical Edition (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: The nāgas take the poison.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: The hālāhala rises first; at the Prajāpatis' plea Śiva, with Pārvatī's assent, drinks it from his palm and it turns his throat blue, 'an ornament of the good'.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

rows.statement: Śiva tells Pārvatī how he drank the kālakūṭa at Brahmā's request and holds it in his throat.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed.; GRETIL e-text

title: Gaṇeśa's birth and elephant head across the Purāṇas
subject: deity:ganesha
question: Who produces Gaṇeśa, and how does he come to have an elephant's head?

rows.statement: Pārvatī shapes an elephant-headed figure from her bath-unguent and throws it into the Gaṅgā; it comes alive as the Gaṅgā's son Gāṅgeya; Brahmā makes him lord of the Vināyakas. No beheading.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: At the gods' request Śiva himself takes the form of an elephant-faced Gaṇeśvara, born of Ambikā, to obstruct the asuras' rites. No beheading.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: A radiant youth springs from Śiva's laughter; jealous when Umā admires him, Śiva curses him to be elephant-faced and pot-bellied; Vināyakas arise from Śiva's sweat.

sources.edition: Varāha Purāṇa (vulgate); Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

rows.statement: Pārvatī makes a door-keeper son from her body's dirt; Śiva beheads him with the trident after a battle; an elephant head (the first one found facing north) is fitted and he is revived and made first-worshipped lord of the gaṇas. The text cites the Śani version as belonging to another kalpa.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

rows.statement: The infant's head falls when Śani looks at him; Viṣṇu cuts the head from a sleeping elephant with his discus and fits it.

sources.edition: Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa (vulgate), Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

note: Courtright (1985) reads the beheading-and-restoration plot as the dominant later form; the Matsya and Liṅga versions without a beheading are generally considered earlier, but none of these chapters is securely dated.

title: What provokes the Narasiṃha manifestation?
subject: narr:narasimha-prahlada
question: Why does Viṣṇu appear as the man-lion, and what is Prahlāda's role?

rows.statement: Hiraṇyakaśipu, made invulnerable by Brahmā's boon, oppresses the gods; at their plea Viṣṇu enters his hall as Narasiṃha and tears him apart. Prahlāda plays no part.

sources.edition: Vaidya CE (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: Brahmā's boon and the gods' appeal again provide the cause; when the man-lion enters the court, Prahlāda alone sees with divine sight that it is the god and warns his father; Narasiṃha kills Hiraṇyakaśipu with his claws.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: The cause is the persecution of Prahlāda for his devotion (poison, serpents, elephants, fire, the sea); the killing by Narasiṃha is only alluded to afterwards (1.20.32).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Framed by the curse of Jaya and Vijaya; Hiraṇyakaśipu seeks revenge for Hiraṇyākṣa, wins Brahmā's boon (7.3.35–38), persecutes Prahlāda, and Narasiṃha emerges from a pillar to prove Prahlāda's word that the Lord is everywhere (7.8.17–29).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

rows.statement: Narasiṃha appears in Hiraṇyakaśipu's city; the king sends his son Prahlāda to kill him; Prahlāda fights, is defeated, then recognises Vāsudeva and urges his father and Hiraṇyākṣa to submit.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Narasiṃha kills Hiraṇyakaśipu but his fury threatens the worlds; Śiva assumes the Śarabha form and subdues him.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

note: Prahlāda's persecution as the trigger is a Vaiṣṇava devotional development (ViP, BhP); the Harivaṃśa and Matsya keep the older deva–asura frame of a boon-proud tyrant.

title: How Viṣṇu acquires the horse's head
subject: deity:hayagriva
question: Why does Viṣṇu take the horse-headed form?

rows.statement: To recover the Vedas stolen by Madhu and Kaiṭabha he assumes the horse-headed form, retrieves them from the underworld, and then kills the demons.

sources.edition: BORI Critical Edition (GRETIL e-text)

rows.statement: Hayaśiras kills Madhu and Kaiṭabha (7.9.37); separately, a demon named Hayagrīva steals the Vedas and is killed by the Fish (8.24).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

rows.statement: A termite created by Brahmā gnaws the bowstring on which the sleeping Viṣṇu rests his chin; the string snaps and cuts off his head; the Goddess has a horse's head fitted so that he can kill the demon Hayagrīva, who could die only at a horse-headed being's hands.

sources.edition: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa (vulgate); Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

title: The seven continents and seven oceans in the Viṣṇu, Bhāgavata and Matsya Purāṇas
subject: place:bhumandala
question: In what order do the continents (dvīpas) and their encircling oceans run outward from Jambudvīpa?

rows.statement: Jambu (salt) — Plakṣa (sugarcane juice) — Śālmala (wine) — Kuśa (ghee) — Krauñca (curds) — Śāka (milk) — Puṣkara (fresh water); then the golden land and Lokāloka.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Jambu (salt) — Plakṣa (sugarcane juice) — Śālmali (wine) — Kuśa (ghee) — Krauñca (milk) — Śāka (curds) — Puṣkara (fresh water); Mānasottara divides Puṣkara; then Lokāloka. The milk and curd oceans are reversed relative to the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

rows.statement: Jambu (salt) — Śāka (milk) — Kuśa (ghee) — Krauñca (curds) — Śālmala (wine) — Gomedaka (sugarcane juice) — Puṣkara (fresh water). No Plakṣa: a Gomedaka continent appears sixth.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

note: Kirfel (1920) groups such variants into recensional families of the Purāṇic 'bhuvanakośa'; all agree on Jambudvīpa at the centre, Puṣkara outermost and seven oceans of different liquids.

title: The names of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas)
subject: place:patala
question: What are the seven worlds below the earth called?

rows.statement: Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat, Mahākhya (Mahātala), Sutala, Pātāla.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner
sources.quote: atalaṃ vitalaṃ caiva nitalaṃ ca gabhastimat / mahākhyaṃ sutalaṃ cāgryaṃ pātālaṃ cāpi saptamam

rows.statement: Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Mahātala, Rasātala, Pātāla; each is described with its inhabitants (Bali in Sutala, Maya in Talātala, the nāgas in Pātāla).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering
sources.quote: atalaṃ vitalaṃ sutalaṃ talātalaṃ mahātalaṃ rasātalaṃ pātālam

rows.statement: In the cosmic body of the Lord (virāṭ), the netherworlds are his feet, ankles and shanks: Pātāla, Rasātala, Mahātala, Talātala…

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering
